title: The disputed history of judicial respect for agency interpretation
shortTitle: The disputed history of judicial respect for agency interpretation
summary: The historical survey distinguishes forms of judicial review and explains why later opinions disagree about what interpretive practice the APA inherited.
notes:
The nineteenth-century account separates common-law damages actions against officers from proceedings for mandamus or injunction. In damages suits, an officer could invoke statutory authority as a defense, and errors could expose the officer to liability. Courts also gave weight to contemporaneous official constructions. In prerogative-writ proceedings, review depended partly on whether the official duty was discretionary or ministerial. Decatur v. Paulding refused mandamus concerning an executive duty involving judgment, while explaining that an ordinary court suit presenting statutory meaning would not bind the Court to the department’s reading. (Printed 928–929.)

The twentieth-century survey identifies both respect for consistent agency practice and a judicial capacity to reject unpersuasive constructions. Burnet emphasized that inconsistency reduced the weight due an executive reading. Gray, Dobson, and Hearst gave particular attention to expert application and mixed questions. Skidmore then articulated persuasion-based factors. Friendly’s later Pittston discussion described analytically conflicting lines of Supreme Court decisions, leaving lower courts to decide which applied. (Printed 929–932.)

Loper Bright’s majority reads this history as a tradition of independent legal interpretation with confined exceptions for delegated factbound questions. Its dissent emphasizes practices around the APA’s enactment that permitted deference and disputes reading § 706 to prohibit a standard already in use. The course account should identify both the form of proceeding and the level of generality at which a historical case is described. The authors’ survey and the Justices’ historical claims are evidence of a disagreement rather than a single settled historical narrative. (Printed 940–944, 957–959, 961–963.)
